intro-statistics-s1.title: A study room at lunch
intro-statistics-s1.html: A high school has 2,400 students. The student council wants to know whether students would use a quiet study room at lunch. The council chooses 120 students at random from the school list and asks each one, "Would you use a quiet study room at lunch once a week or more?" Of the 120 students, 78 answer yes (invented data).

intro-statistics-s2.title: Sleep on school nights
intro-statistics-s2.html: A health teacher wants to learn how many hours of sleep students in her district get on school nights. The district has 6 high schools with 9,000 students in all. She asks 60 students from her own school, each in one of her classes, to record their sleep for one week (invented data).

items.q: What is the population in this study?

why.correct: The population is the whole group the question is about: all 2,400 students at the school.
options: These 120 are the sample: the part of the population the council actually asked.
Right: the question is about every student at the school, so the whole school is the population.
The 78 are a count inside the sample, not the group the question is about.
The question is about every student, not just those who already use a study space.
The 120 students chosen from the school list
All 2,400 students at the school
The 78 students who answered yes to the question
Students who already study in the library at lunch

items.q: What is the sample in this study?

why.correct: The sample is the part of the population that data come from: the 120 students who were asked.
options: That is the population, the whole group the question is about.
They are part of the sample, but the sample is everyone who was asked, yes or no.
The council ran the study; they are not the students who were asked.
Right: the sample is the group data were actually collected from.
The 2,400 students enrolled at the high school
The 78 students who said they would use the room
The members of the student council who ran the study
The 120 students the council asked

items.q: Which statement correctly uses the data?

why.correct: The 78 yes answers are 78 out of 120, which is 65% of the sample. That is a fact about the sample and an estimate for the school.
options: Right: 78 out of 120 is 0.65, and it describes the students who were asked.
The 65% describes the sample. A different sample would give a slightly different number, so it is not exact for the whole school.
78 is the count of yes answers, not a percent: 78 out of 120 is 65%.
Just 120 of the 2,400 students were asked; far more than 78 students at the school could want the room.
65% of the students asked said yes
Exactly 65% of the school’s 2,400 students would use the room
78% of the students at the school would use the study room
Exactly 78 students at the school would use the study room

items.q: A second group of 120 students is chosen at random from the same school list and asked the same question. What is most likely?

why.correct: Different students give different answers, so a new group of 120 gives a result that varies a little from the first one but is usually close to it.
options: Different students are chosen each time, so the count changes from group to group even when the school stays the same.
Groups chosen by chance from the same school tend to give similar results; a huge change would be surprising.
Right: answers vary from student to student, so each group of 120 gives a somewhat different percent, usually close to the first.
The method is the same, but the students are different, so the result usually shifts a little.
Exactly 78 yes answers, because the school itself has not changed
A percent very far from 65%, since each group is chosen by chance
A percent near 65%, but probably not exactly 65%
Exactly 65% of the 120, because the method of choosing is the same

items.q: What population does the teacher want to learn about?

why.correct: The population is the group the question is about: all 9,000 high school students in the district.
options: These 60 are the sample she collected data from.
Her question names the district, so the population is every high school student in the district.
Right: her question is about students in the whole district.
Her question is about one district, not every teenager.
The 60 students in her classes who kept sleep records
The students who attend her own high school
The district’s 9,000 high school students
Teenagers across the country who go to high school

items.q: Why might her 60 students give a poor picture of the population?

why.correct: A sample is useful when it looks like the population. Students from one school, and from one teacher’s classes, may sleep differently from students across the district.
options: Right: a sample tells about a population only when it represents it, and this one leaves out five of the six schools.
Sixty is a manageable number; the problem is who the 60 are, not how many.
Students can record when they fall asleep and wake up; the measurement is possible.
A week of records covers several school nights, which helps; the trouble is which students were chosen.
They come from one school, so they may sleep differently from students elsewhere
Sixty students is too many people for one teacher to measure carefully
Hours of sleep are too personal to measure, so the records are guesses
One week is too long a time to keep a record of sleep for each student

items.q: Which question can her data help answer, with the data collected as described?

why.correct: Data answer questions about the group they come from. Her records describe the students in her classes.
options: That has one exact answer from one record; it is not a question about a group with answers that vary.
She has no data from the other schools, so she has nothing to compare.
That is a fact to look up, not a question answered by collecting data that vary.
Right: the data come from her classes, so they describe her classes well.
How many hours did one particular student in her class sleep last Tuesday night?
Do students at the other five schools sleep less than the students in her classes?
What time does the first class at her school start each school morning?
How much do students in her classes sleep on school nights?

items.q: To learn about the whole district, which change to her plan helps most?

why.correct: To learn about a population, the sample has to come from the whole population. Choosing at random from a district list does that.
options: More nights from the same students still leaves out the other five schools.
Right: choosing by chance from the whole district gives every school a fair place in the sample.
A bigger sample from one school still does not represent the other five schools.
Changing the students’ sleep would ruin the measurement of their usual sleep.
Ask the same 60 students to keep records for two weeks instead of one
Choose students at random from a district list
Ask 200 students from her own school instead of 60 from her classes
Ask her students to go to bed earlier during the week of the study

items.q: Which question is answered by collecting data that vary from one person to another?

why.correct: Statistics answers questions where the answers vary, so the data must come from many individuals.
options: Right: homework time differs from student to student, so it takes data from many students to answer.
That is one number about one person; there is no variation to study.
The lunch period has one fixed length; looking it up answers the question.
That is one fixed number from the school records, not data that vary.
How long do students here spend on homework on a typical night?
How many minutes did I spend on my own homework last night?
How many minutes long is the lunch period at this school?
How many students are enrolled at this school this year?

why.correct: A sample is the part of the population you collect data from.
options: That describes the population.
That is a conclusion, not a group of people or things.
Right: a sample is a subset of the population.
The question comes first; the sample is who or what you collect data from.
The whole group of people or things that the question is about
The answer that a study reports about the group it studied
The part of the population that data come from
The question that the researchers are trying to answer

items.q: A quality team weighs 50 bags of rice taken from a day’s production of 8,000 bags. What is the population?

why.correct: The population is every bag the question is about: all 8,000 made that day.
options: These are the sample.
Right: the team wants to know about the whole day’s production.
That is a label, not a group of bags.
The machine makes the bags; the question is about the bags themselves.
The 50 bags that the team took and weighed
The 8,000 bags made that day
The weight that is printed on each bag of rice
The machine on the line that fills the bags

items.q: A park department asks 300 park visitors whether they want more shade trees; 210 say yes. Which conclusion is stated in context?

why.correct: A conclusion in context names who was studied, what was measured, and what the number tells you: 210 out of 300 is 70% of the visitors surveyed.
options: A number with no context does not say who, or what the 70% measures.
This does not name the people, the park or the trees.
True arithmetic, but it says nothing about the visitors or the trees.
Right: it says who was asked, what about, and the number: 210 out of 300 is 70%.
The answer to the question is 70%, which is more than half
Most of the people who answered the question want more of it
210 is greater than 300 divided by 2, so the result is a majority
70% of the 300 visitors asked want more shade trees

items.q: A town wants to know how residents feel about a new bike lane. Why ask a sample of residents instead of every resident?

why.correct: Collecting data from everyone takes time and money. A sample that represents the town gives a useful estimate at a fraction of the cost.
options: A sample gives an estimate; another sample would give a slightly different result.
Right: a good sample can stand in for the population at a small part of the cost.
Everyone may have an opinion; they simply are not asked.
The reason is practical: time and cost, not a rule.
A sample gives the exact answer for the whole town, with no error
It is faster and cheaper, and a good sample still describes the town
Residents who are not chosen for the sample have no opinion to give
Towns are required by law to ask a sample and not the whole town

items.q: A news site asks its readers to vote online on whether the city should build a stadium. Of 5,000 votes, 80% say no. What is the main problem with saying "80% of city residents oppose the stadium"?

why.correct: A result describes the population only when the sample represents it. People who choose to answer may differ from everyone else.
options: Five thousand is a large number; the problem is who voted, not how many.
Percents describe opinions well; the issue is whose opinions they are.
Recounting would not fix who took part in the vote.
Right: the people who voted picked themselves, and they may feel more strongly or differ from residents in other ways.
5,000 votes is far too few to learn anything about a whole city
Percents are a poor way to describe opinions about a stadium
The votes should have been counted a second time to be sure
Readers who chose to vote may not represent the city

items.q: A researcher measures the heights of 40 sunflowers chosen from a field of 2,000 sunflowers. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

why.correct: The population is the field of 2,000; the sample is the 40 measured. Heights vary, and the sample gives an estimate for the field.
options: Right: the question is about the whole field.
Right: data come from these 40.
Heights vary from plant to plant; that variation is why many plants are measured.
The 40 give an estimate for the field, not an exact value.
The 2,000 sunflowers are the population
The 40 measured sunflowers are the sample
The 40 measured heights will be identical
The field’s heights are known exactly from the 40

items.q: Which is the best reason to report results "in context"?

why.correct: Context tells the reader whom the data describe and what was measured, so the number can be understood and used.
options: Right: a number says little until you know whom and what it describes.
Context does not change precision; it explains the meaning.
Rounding is a different choice; context is about meaning.
Length is not the goal; meaning is.
So a reader knows who was studied and what was measured
So that the numbers in the report look more precise to a reader
Because results should be rounded to whole percents before they are shared
To make the written report longer and more detailed for the reader

items.q: A coach asks, "Do the players on my team who stretch before practice get fewer injuries?" Which data would help answer this?

why.correct: To answer a question about a group, collect data on every individual that measure what the question names: stretching and injuries.
options: The team size alone says nothing about stretching or injuries.
One player does not show how stretching and injuries relate across a team.
Right: the question compares injuries for stretchers and non-stretchers, so both facts are needed for every player.
The exercises do not tell who stretched or who was injured.
The number of players on the team and the number of practices
The full injury history of the best player on the team this season
For each player: stretches or not, and number of injuries
The names of the stretching exercises the team does before practice
